description: I want to create a public-facing app to display images of the sky from the SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time. Users will enter the coordinates of a patch of sky (Right Ascension and declination).
summary: This is an interactive web application that converts NASA’s SPHEREx sky data from their space telescope into time-lapse animation of rolling Solar Energetic Particles (SEPs) (75 and 5.0 microns), time-lapse of aligned rolling SEPs, or stacks of aligned data from all detectors. Sky Gazer helps people to investigate the whole depth of the NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey through converting complex data from NASA’s IRSA and MAST archives, alignment of exposures (rotations included), propagation of positions of high proper motion stars to coincide with observation epochs, removal of zodiacal background and, whenever applicable, high-resolution data from MAST archives to increase sharpness of images. People may use the application to get time-lapse animation of variable stars, stars, brown dwarfs and moving objects or to produce stacks of data.
details:
What it does and how it works When a user enters a sky coordinate and cutout radius in the Streamlit interface, SkyGazer's backend (spherex.py) searches NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive (spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3) via SIA and TAP queries. When IRSA's search proxy is overloaded and returns 502 Proxy Errors, the pipeline automatically switches to a deterministic bypass: it calculates the target's exact HEALPix Norder=5 nested pixel ID (Npix) in Python, streams the matching SPHEREx DR1 All-Sky HiPS spectral cube directly from NASA's public AWS S3 bucket (nasa-irsa-spherex), caches the cube locally, and crops 2D FITS cutouts across detectors D1–D6 using Astropy's World Coordinate System (WCS) and Cutout2D. SkyGazer then plots surface brightness (MJy/sr) across wavelength and maps those spectral values into a playable audio waveform.

Benefits and intended impact Raw infrared spectroscopy is normally locked behind specialized FITS tools, multi-extension headers, and heavy downloads that discourage beginners. SkyGazer removes that barrier by turning any patch of sky into visual cutouts, an easy-to-read spectrum, and sound in one interface. Our goal is to make NASA's all-sky SPHEREx survey accessible to students, educators, amateur astronomers, and visually impaired users who can explore astronomical objects by ear.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used

  • Language: Python 3
  • Astronomy & scientific libraries: astropy (SkyCoord, fits, WCS, Cutout2D, Table, Time, votable), astroquery (Irsa), numpy
  • Data transport & spatial indexing: requests (chunked HTTP streaming with local disk caching) and a custom pure-Python HEALPix nested pixel mapper (Norder=5, nside=32)
  • Frontend & audio: Streamlit for the interactive web interface and Python waveform synthesis for spectral sonification
  • NASA data & cloud infrastructure: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) and NASA SPHEREx Open Data on AWS S3
  • Hardware: Standard consumer laptop with local SSD storage for caching FITS spectral cubes

How our project is creative Instead of treating SPHEREx data only as static tables or grayscale FITS frames, SkyGazer combines multi-band infrared imaging ($0.75\text{–}5.0\ \mu\text{m}$) with audio sonification so users can hear how brightness changes from near-infrared to mid-infrared wavelengths. On the engineering side, pairing official IRSA queries with a math-driven HEALPix-to-AWS-S3 failover keeps the app working even during live archive outages.

Factors our team considered

  • Outage resilience: Live IRSA /SIA and /TAP/sync queries frequently drop connections with 502 errors during traffic spikes, so we built multi-tier failover directly to NASA's S3 mirror.
  • Download speed and local caching: Streaming a ~320 MB spectral cube repeatedly is slow, so SkyGazer downloads each sky tile once into data/raw/spherex/_cubes/ and slices repeat searches locally in under a second.
  • Instrument data quirks: SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cubes leave dichroic crossover channels 50 and 51 blank, so our pipeline filters them out automatically and spaces samples evenly across detectors D1–D6.
  • Usability: We built simple coordinate inputs, detector filters, and preset targets so someone with zero FITS or Python background can run a query immediately.
